title: What is DVGW certification? A guide for Indian manufacturers
summary: What DVGW is, why German buyers ask for it and how the certification works, in plain language.

body.p: If you have spoken to a German utility, wholesaler or OEM about supplying valves, pipes, fittings or meters, you have almost certainly been asked: "Is it DVGW certified?" This article explains what that question means.

DVGW (Deutscher Verein des Gas- und Wasserfaches e.V.) is the German technical and scientific association that sets the rules for the drinking-water sector. Founded in 1859, it writes the technical rules, the DVGW worksheets (Arbeitsblätter), that German water utilities follow. Its certification body, DVGW CERT GmbH, certifies products against these rules and the related European standards.

German utilities and installers rely on the "generally accepted rules of technology". A DVGW certificate is the most widely recognised evidence that a product meets them. Without it, many tenders and distributor listings are simply not accessible.

ul: Review of the technical documentation
Type testing of product samples at an accredited laboratory
An initial inspection of the factory production control
Evaluation and issue of the certificate
Regular surveillance to keep the certificate valid

body.p: The process typically takes 6 to 12 months. Preparation is the factor you can influence most.

title: Drinking-water hygiene: understanding the UBA evaluation criteria
summary: Why the materials in your product matter as much as its performance, and how the German Environment Agency's criteria affect certification.

body.p: The German Drinking Water Ordinance (TrinkwV) requires that materials in contact with drinking water do not harm water quality. The German Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt, UBA) defines binding evaluation criteria for organic materials, metals, and cementitious and enamel materials.

ul: Every wetted component counts, including O-rings, lubricants and coatings.
Metallic materials must appear on the UBA list of approved metallic materials. For brass, lead content is critical.
Organic materials such as elastomers and plastics need evidence of conformity, usually from the compound supplier.

body.p: Before designing your test programme, build a wetted-materials bill of materials and check each item. Choosing approved compounds early avoids months of delay.

title: The 10-document certification preparation guide
summary: The documents every certification body will ask for, and how to prepare each one properly.

body.p: Incomplete or inconsistent documents are the most common cause of delay. These ten document groups form the core of almost every DVGW application.

ul: Company registration and legal entity details
Product datasheets for the complete range in scope
Revision-controlled technical drawings
Material specifications for all wetted components
Quality certificates such as ISO 9001
Existing test reports and approvals
Manufacturing process documentation and control plan
Product images and marking
Inspection and calibration records
Factory information for the audit

body.p: The drawings, the samples and the datasheets must describe the same product. Certification bodies check this carefully.

title: Exporting industrial water products from India to Germany
summary: Market structure, buyer expectations and the documents you need beyond certification.

body.p: Germany is Europe's largest market for water infrastructure products. Its buyers are demanding, loyal and highly standards-driven.

ul: Municipal utilities (Stadtwerke) and water associations, often through public tenders
Specialist wholesalers serving installers
OEMs integrating components into larger systems
German-language technical documentation and installation instructions
CE marking where EU directives or regulations apply
Reliable delivery and spare-parts availability
A local point of contact for technical questions

body.p: Certification opens the door. Service quality and documentation keep it open.

title: DVGW certification vs. CE marking: what's the difference?
summary: Two different systems with different purposes. Many products need both.

body.p: CE marking shows conformity with EU legislation such as the Machinery Regulation, the Pressure Equipment Directive or the Measuring Instruments Directive. Where the law requires it, it is mandatory.

DVGW certification shows conformity with German technical rules and the relevant European product standards, including hygiene requirements for drinking water. It is market-driven and widely expected.

A pump sold for drinking-water use in Germany will usually need CE marking for machinery safety and evidence of hygiene and suitability, typically a DVGW certificate. A water meter needs MID conformity and benefits from DVGW evidence of material hygiene.

title: Preparing your factory for the initial inspection
summary: What German auditors look for in factory production control, and how to prepare your team.

body.p: The initial inspection confirms that your factory can consistently produce the product that was tested. Auditors focus on control, traceability and records.

ul: Incoming material inspection and supplier control
Process control at critical steps
Calibrated measuring and test equipment
Final inspection and release testing
Traceability from raw material to the finished product
Handling of non-conforming products and complaints

body.p: A mock audit two to four weeks before the real one, run against the certification body's checklist, is the most effective preparation.

title: Industry update: the revised German Drinking Water Ordinance
summary: The 2023 revision of the TrinkwV and what it means for suppliers of drinking-water products.

body.p: Germany's revised Drinking Water Ordinance came into force in 2023, implementing the EU Drinking Water Directive (EU) 2020/2184. It reinforces risk-based approaches and the binding role of the UBA evaluation criteria for materials.

At EU level, harmonised requirements for materials in contact with drinking water are being introduced step by step. Manufacturers should monitor the transition periods that apply to their materials and products.
ESC tracks these developments and briefs clients on their impact on certifications already held or in progress.

body.p: This white paper sets out a four-phase framework: Assess, Prepare, Certify and Enter. It is built on lessons from Indo-German projects in the utility sector.
Choose the right products for Germany, map the applicable rules and build a business case.
Freeze designs, qualify materials, complete the documentation and pre-test.
Manage the laboratory testing and factory inspection with a single coordinator.
Localise documentation, build distributor relationships and prepare for tenders.

title: Case study (illustrative): brass ball valves for German building installations
summary: How a mid-sized valve manufacturer could prepare a ball-valve range for certification, with a materials issue resolved before testing.

body.p: Note: this is a representative scenario that shows a typical project flow. It does not describe a specific client.
A manufacturer of brass ball valves (DN 15 to DN 50) wanted to supply a German wholesaler that required DVGW certification.

ul: The brass alloy in use was not on the UBA list of approved metallic materials.
The seat-seal compound had no drinking-water evidence.
The drawings lacked revision control.

body.p: The manufacturer switched to an approved low-lead brass alloy, qualified a seal compound from an approved supplier and introduced document control. Samples went to the laboratory only after successful in-house pre-tests.
Testing completed without re-tests, and the factory inspection closed with minor findings only.

title: Case study (illustrative): PE 100 pressure pipes for water distribution
summary: A representative pipe-manufacturer project that used an approved compound to shorten the certification route.

body.p: Note: this is a representative scenario that shows a typical project flow. It does not describe a specific client.
A PE pipe extruder wanted to enter German water distribution projects with PE 100 pipes in the SDR 11 and SDR 17 series.

ul: Choose a PE 100 compound with existing approvals
Select representative dimensions for type testing
Establish batch traceability and marking
Prepare factory production control for the initial inspection

body.p: Planning the long-term hydrostatic tests early let the project run in parallel with factory preparation rather than one after the other.

title: Seven common mistakes that delay DVGW certification
summary: Lessons from the field: the avoidable issues that cost manufacturers months.

ul: Starting testing before the design is frozen
Ignoring the hygiene evidence for small wetted parts
Drawings that don't match the samples
Grouping product variants poorly
Changing suppliers mid-process
Underestimating long-term tests
Treating the factory audit as a formality

body.p: Each of these can be avoided with a structured readiness assessment at the start.

title: Water meters: navigating MID approval and DVGW requirements
summary: How metrological approval and hygiene certification fit together for water-meter manufacturers.

body.p: Water meters sold in the EU for billing must conform to the Measuring Instruments Directive (2014/32/EU), assessed by a notified body against EN ISO 4064 / OIML R 49.
German utilities additionally expect evidence of material hygiene and suitability for the German water supply. Planning both routes together avoids duplicate testing.

ul: Start the MID type examination and the hygiene evidence in parallel
Use the same samples where the test programmes allow
Align the quality-system module with the factory inspection
